data.title: Hedge fund Two Sigma ends real estate unit fundraising, cuts staff - report
data.description:
Quantitative hedge fund Two Sigma Investments has halted efforts to raise $2B for its real estate investment unit and cut senior staff, as rising interest rates hobbled its fundraising efforts, according to a media report on Friday.

The unit's partner and chief investment officer, Rich Gomel, is leaving the company. Others on the real estate leadership team, including two of the three remaining partners and one of the two heads of data science, are also departing, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The firm, which had targeted raising ~$2B for the business, pulled in less than half that amount, some of the people told Bloomberg. Some of the real estate team will remain to manage its existing portfolio of properties.

Rising interest rates have weighed on commercial property valuations and led to owners holding assets for longer. Bloomberg, citing data from PEI Group, noted that private real estate fundraising totaled just over $30B for Q3 2026, the lowest quarterly total since early 2013.

Two Sigma started forming the real estate business in 2019 and launched it with internal capital about two years later. It was led by former Blackstone Vice Chair Tom Hill, who left the firm last year, one of the people told Bloomberg.

The business started taking outside capital in 2024 with its Real Estate Opportunity Fund, which mostly focused on housing and industrial investments, with some selective stakes in hospitality and office real estate. The hedge fund's strategy was to use the firm's data to power predictive tools that could project supply and demand, which would determine investment decisions.

data.title: Cogent Comm drops on report it hired advisor on refinancing concerns, S&P downgrade

Biggest stock movers Friday: Chips stocks, CRWV, and more
data.description:
Stock futures were mixed on Friday as Wall Street builds on the prior session's recovery from an earlier AI-driven tech sell-off, pointing to a positive finish for the week.

Here are some of Friday's biggest stock movers:

Biggest stock gainers

  • SITE Centers (SITC) +18% - Shares surged after the retail real estate investment trust announced plans to voluntarily delist its common shares from the New York Stock Exchange following a special distribution declared on Oct. 15, 2026. The company expects the delisting to take effect before trading begins on Dec. 4, 2026, and said it has not arranged for its shares to trade on another exchange or quotation platform.
  • Cohen & Steers (CNS) +2% - Shares climbed following the release of mixed Q3 results, with total revenue rising 11% Y/Y. The quarter was propelled by $1.6B in broad-based net inflows, representing the strongest quarterly inflow performance since the fourth quarter of 2021, though total assets under management closed at $95.9B, down 4.2% sequentially due to $5.1B in market depreciation. Growth was bolstered by continued momentum across wealth channels, including mutual funds, SICAVs, and the newly launched Cohen & Steers Real Assets Active ETF (CSRA).

Biggest stock losers

  • Omeros (OMER) -12% - Shares plummeted after the European Medicines Agency's Committee for Medicinal Products for Human Use (CHMP) issued a second negative opinion on the marketing authorization application for its stem cell transplant therapy, narsoplimab. The decision followed a formal re-examination of an initial negative opinion adopted in June. Seattle-based Omeros noted that patient-level data submitted in August was excluded from the ad hoc expert panel’s reevaluation, despite meeting minutes recommending an external expert review of that data. Narsoplimab, marketed in the U.S. as Yartemlea for stem cell transplant-associated thrombotic microangiopathy, continues its U.S. commercial rollout. Separately, Omeros announced plans to wind down its European compassionate-use program to prioritize escalating U.S. commercial demand.
  • CoreWeave (CRWV) -5% - Shares slipped despite Cantor Fitzgerald encouraging investors to "buy the dip." Cantor analyst Brett Knoblauch reiterated an Overweight rating and a $176 price target, dismissing recent market concern over CoreWeave's leverage as excessive fearmongering. Knoblauch emphasized that CoreWeave's hardware revenue capacity has nearly doubled to $20 million per megawatt with 25–30% contribution margins, compressing payback cycles on GPU investments to 2–2.5 years. However, investor anxiety remains heightened following a 15% debt-fueled equity plunge earlier in the week, compounded by a Gartner research report forecasting that 80% of independent neocloud providers could cease standalone operations by 2030 due to capital intensity.
  • Micron (MU) -3% - Semiconductor equities slid across the board Friday, threatening to extend the sector's losing streak to an eighth consecutive session as persistent fears over high borrowing costs and AI infrastructure spending drag down high-beta tech names. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) fell nearly 1%, led lower by memory and hardware heavyweights including Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) and SanDisk (SNDK), which dropped 3% each. Broad-based selling hit chipmakers across the board, with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), Broadcom (AVGO), Lam Research (LRCX), and Intel (INTC) each shedding 2% as institutional investors continued trimming risk exposure across logic and hardware suppliers.

data.title: Global diesel will remain expensive even as crude prices lower – analyst
data.description:
High global diesel prices and supply constraints are set to persist even as crude oil prices (CL1:COM), (CO1:COM) soften, according to Daan Struyven, Goldman Sachs co-head of global commodities research.

In an interview with CNBC, Struyven noted that Goldman Sachs expects "somewhat lower crude prices" going forward but warned of "very high product prices for longer."

U.S. average retail diesel prices recently hit an all-time high of $6.50 a gallon and remain just above $6, creating significant economic headwinds.

Struyven described diesel as the "workhorse fuel of the global economy," explaining that unlike gasoline (XB1:COM) and jet fuel, "it has a very broad-based impact on many CPI categories."

The effects also take longer to materialize, with economic lags extending the timeline for price pressures to work through the system.

The ongoing diesel market tightness stems from multiple compounding supply issues, with the market only receiving roughly 30% of normal product volumes through the Strait of Hormuz and out of the Persian Gulf.

Additionally, Russian diesel exports remain severely depressed, and the diesel and refining market "were very tight coming into this year in contrast to the crude market."

Even if shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz fully reopen, market relief will be limited. "It would provide some incremental easing, but the market would remain tight," Struyven said, highlighting the structural nature of the supply imbalances.

The International Energy Agency announced plans to release over 20 million barrels of diesel—roughly five days of U.S. consumption—while cautioning that constraints on diesel could continue into next year.

Struyven noted that prolonged elevated fuel prices carry implications for monetary policy, pointing out that Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Walsh recently mentioned crack spreads at his FOMC press conference.

The strong central bank response to fuel prices helps explain why bond and equity prices have become "unusually correlated with energy prices," Struyven added, noting that resilient economic conditions and five years of inflation overshooting targets have given central bankers room to respond forcefully.

data.title: Tesla-SpaceX merger timeline draws sharper focus after Roadster debut
data.description:
Prediction market traders have lifted the odds of a Tesla (TSLA)-SpaceX (SPCX) merge, with Kalshi contracts now pricing a greater-than-even chance of a deal by spring 2027 following the electric-vehicle maker’s Roadster showcase.

The market assigns a 15% probability of a merger before December 1, 2026, rising to 26% before January 1, 2027, 34% before February 1, and 39% before March 1. Probabilities then move above 50%, reaching 57% before April 1, 59% before May 1, and 77% before 2028. 

The shift comes after Tesla unveiled its next-generation Roadster at a SpaceX facility in McGregor, Texas. The prototype, developed with SpaceX engineering input, used compressed-air cold-gas thrusters for short airborne maneuvers, including an inverted ramp run, mid-air flips, and a controlled landing, while separate runs posted 0-60 mph times as quick as 0.81 seconds. Production remains targeted for 2028. 

Wall Street notes have added to the timeline discussion. Barclays analysts have suggested an announcement could arrive ahead of Tesla’s annual shareholder meeting, which must occur by December 6, potentially structured around AI and robotics integration spanning robotaxis, Optimus, and related platforms. 

While the companies have long collaborated under Elon Musk, the combination of the Roadster demonstration, rising Kalshi probabilities, and recent research commentary has sharpened attention on whether operational overlap could progress into a formal transaction in the months and quarters ahead.

data.title: Prudential Financial estimates $140M hit to Q3 earnings from Japan
data.description:
In disclosing some preliminary Q3 measures, Prudential Financial (PRU) estimated that the suspension of sales at Prudential Japan will reduce its Japan businesses' pretax adjusted operating income by ~$140M in Q3 2026.

The disclosure came late Thursday in a filing ahead of the company's full Q3 earnings report to be released after the market close on Nov. 3, 2026.

The estimated reduction to income includes one-time costs primarily related to Life Planner compensation, lost sales, and the impact of surrenders.

That's part of Prudential's (PRU) previous estimate that the suspension of sales for some products in Japan would reduce pretax adjusted operating income by a total of ~$1BB across 2026 and 2027, including $500M in 2026 and $500-$550M in 2027.

In other preliminary Q3 metrics, Prudential's (PRU) PGIM segment assets under management were $1.47T at Sept. 30, 2026, down from the $1.49T at June 30.

The company also estimated that the alternative investment income of its general account, excluding the closed block division and funds withheld portfolio, was ~$15M-$35M above its near-term expectations during Q3.

Prudential Financial (PRU) stock edged up 0.3% in Friday morning trading.

Initially, Prudential had, in February, voluntarily suspended POJ's new sales activity for 90 days, then extended it by an additional 180 days after it had discovered employee misconduct at the unit, including some employees making inappropriate investment solicitations.

Earlier this month, Japan's Financial Services Agency extended the period in which Prudential of Japan cannot solicit new business until Jan. 31, 2027. It also orders a business suspension through the same date for the Life Consultant channel of Prudential's Gibraltar Life unit.

data.title: Batteries to thrusters: Tesla's 18-year road to the flying car
data.description:
Over eighteen turbulent years, Elon Musk transformed Tesla (TSLA) from a niche garage venture re-engineering sports cars into an industry-shattering titan preparing to literally launch vehicles into the air.

The trajectory started in 2008 with the original Roadster, a hand-assembled proof-of-concept built on a Lotus Elise glider that nearly bankrupted the startup before proving battery power could outperform internal combustion. 

That high-cost experiment generated the capital and credibility needed to design the Model S in 2012 and the falcon-winged Model X in 2015, effectively redefining modern luxury vehicles as software-driven supercomputers on wheels.

Musk’s mainstream takeover followed with the mass-market Model 3 sedan in 2017 and the Model Y crossover in 2020.

Recent years have marked a pivot toward radical geometry and autonomy. The angular, stainless-steel Cybertruck arrived in 2023 as an uncompromising break from traditional utility design, followed by the steering-wheel-free Cybercab, cementing Tesla's (TSLA) bet on automated mobility networks over traditional driver ownership.

The fleet’s evolution now circles back to its origins with the second-generation Roadster, which features thrusters designed to enable short flights. Tesla (TSLA) held its Roadster event at a SpaceX (SPCX) testing facility in McGregor, Texas, on Thursday night, with Musk saying the next-gen model is the result of a cutting-edge electric vehicle manufacturer working with a leading rocket engine maker.

data.title: U.S. steel prices surge to four-year highs as overseas supplies decline sharply
data.description:
The steel sector is set to report Q3 earnings in the coming days and weeks that analysts expect will show higher sales and profits, as U.S. steel prices have climbed to more than four-year highs.

U.S. tariffs on imported steel are restricting foreign supply, which has helped boost U.S. hot-rolled coil prices by 52% over the past year to $1,255/short ton, the highest level since May 2022, Bloomberg reported Friday.

The U.S. is a net importer of steel but deliveries of overseas supplies have declined sharply this year, as imports of finished steel fell 14% YTD to ~13M tons, resulting in a slide of imports' share of the domestic market to 16% from 19% for the same period last year, according to the American Iron and Steel Institute.

Analysts expect domestic supplies will tighten heading into the end of the year as mills curb activity to perform routine maintenance; more than 1M tons of production is forecast to be affected in the September-December period, Fastmarkets said.

Steel buyers should expect prices to continue ticking higher, and contract negotiations between producers and customers for 2027 "so far are favoring mills and are likely to be at lower discounts than recent years," Bloomberg Intelligence senior analyst Richard Bourke said.

U.S. steel producers including Nucor (NUE), Steel Dynamics (STLD), and Cleveland-Cliffs (CLF) have benefited from stronger domestic pricing and reduced foreign competition, and their respective stocks are trading up 3.3%, 2.9%, and 3.2% on Friday.
